full_judgment:
4. However, I propose to take up first the case of contemner No.1 Mr. Ashok K Karmaker. The article covering 6 columns is on the power and ability of the Judges of the High Court Division to issue Rule and the order passed in exercise of their power under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 6. I am conscious about self-imposed limitation in dealing with contempt of Court matter by the learned Judges of the Superior Court. There is a long constructive criticism of the judgment is no offence and does not call for initiation of the Contempt proceeding as the judiciary improves upon constructive and corrective criticism made bona fide of a judgment. In this regard, I may profitably quote the following illuminating observation of Lord Denning made in the famous Quintin Hogg Case (1958) 2 WLR 1206: "It is the right of every man in Parliament or out of it, in the press or over the broadcast, to make fair comment, even outspoken comment, on matters of public interest. Those who comment can deal faithfully with all that is done in a court of justice, ................. silence is not an option when things are ill done. The Supreme Court of India in Special Reference No. 1 of 1964, 1965 (SC) 745 aptly observed: "We ought not to forget that the power to punish for contempt large as it is, must always be exercised consciously, wisely and with circumspection. Frequent and indiscriminate use of this power in anger or irritation would not help to sustain the dignity or the status of the court but may sometimes affect it adversely. In the light of the aforesaid observations the expressions used by the writer in his article is to be considered. The article was written and published after issuance of the Rules following resignation of 149 Members of the Parliament in Writ Petitions 88 and 161 of 1995 and also with reference to certain order of the learned Judges of this Division made in another Contempt proceeding (presumably Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 835 of 1993-Cyril Skikder vs. Mr. Nazmul Huda). The offending article contains, inter alia, "But soon after their entering upon the office the MPs, particularly belonging to the Treasury Bench, started voicing against the judiciary. And the judiciary also did not lag behind in this competition when it came forward to play an offensive role with an instrument (the contempt of court proceedings) which is really meant and created for its defence. "The writer further proceeded to write" In the last attempt the High Court served show cause notice upon the Speaker and asked him not to pass any ruling for the time being regarding resignation of opposition MPs. And the Speaker also did not hesitate to make it public that order of the High Court would not debar him from passing the ruling on the issue. There is no doubt the jurisdiction of the Court is vast. but should it be wide enough to reach out to the Parliament also? The answer obviously should be and must be a resolute No. 

 7. The writer also wrote with reference to a contempt proceeding regarding the Judges of this Division imputing inability and lack of courage. He writes: The High Court Division served show cause notice upon the then Information Minister and later in pursuance to the doctrine one step forward two steps back, it retreated and recalled the notice." He further writes, the Judges are appointed by the people and entrusted with certain power to adjudicate. But going to discharge our duties we cannot rob the people of the right which exclusively belongs to them. lf we can be called formal Judges the people are informal Judges and are much more powerful than the formal ones. There must be some limitations and it is also true with the judiciary. But in no way does it mean that at the time of national crisis the judiciary would overlook it or become a mere onlooker. Only the spineless or utter indifferent can do so. We really do not need such spineless men as Judges. (Emphasis supplied). Even from a cursory reading of the above passages it is seen that the writer took upon himself gratuitous responsibility of advising the learned Judges only to expose them in a scandalous manner to the society at the time when the High Court Division was seriously dealing with the Constitutional matter in a sensitive atmosphere prevailing in the country during pendency of hearing of the Rules issued by the High Court Division in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. From the quoted passages it becomes manifestly clear that it tends to interfere with the administration of justice. Writing with such a tone by a member of the Subordinate Judicial Service is the grossest type of scandalising of the Judges of the Supreme Court. Before issuance of the Rule we enquired from" the Registrar of the Supreme Court as to whether the writer took permission from the authority to write the article. From the Registrar of the Supreme Court we learnt that Mr. Ashok K Karmaker did not obtain any permission from the Government for writing the article. Such a contemptuous writing without permission from the authority on the part of a judicial officer is also offence. However, that is for the Executive Branch of the Government for taking necessary action. The expressions "offensive role and only the spineless or utter indifferent can do so. We really do not need such spineless judges "employed by the writer clearly are the outcome of much deliberation calculated to scandalise the judges of the highest judiciary of the country. Silence is no good sign for a strong judiciary where such a scandalous writing appears in an article in the newspaper. A bona fide and honest criticism of the judiciary is called for only when it is aimed for improvement of its quality by way of constructive criticism but by using the words" If we can be called formal judges, the people are informal judges. And, as as matter of fact the informal judges are much more powerful than the formal ones" are the uttered words of warning for the Judges. That they have "limitations" are remarks with a motive to scandalise the Judge. This is not, in fact, a corrective criticism of the judgment. It is not understood from where the writer, a member of judiciary, got such an inspiration and courage to attack the highest judiciary in this type of scandalous writing. This article as is full of contumacious writing from a member of the Subordinate Judicial Service hardly deserves a lenient and generous consideration and the test, "The dogs may bark, the caravan will pass" of Krishna Ayer, J should not be adhered to. And if it is so shown it would be a premium given to a member of Subordinate Judiciary. This view finds support from the decision in the case Sir Edward Snelson vs. The Judges of the High Court of West Pakistan, 16 DLR 535 (SC) to which I shall refer and quote presently briefly after narrating the facts of that case. Sir Edward Snelson was the Secretary of the Ministry of Law of the Government of Pakistan. While addressing the Section Officers of the erstwhile Pakistan he made certain observations with regard to the power of the Supreme Court and the High Courts of Pakistan to issue writ after proclamation of Martial Law by the Military Ruler General Ayub Khan of Pakistan. The offending passages contained in the talk were printed in pamphlets entitled" The Transitional Constitution of 1958" copy of which was forwarded to the Registrar, High Court of West Pakistan, Lahore. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in this case dealt in a great detail and almost all aspects of law of contempt were considered as the contemner defended himself. But as in the instant case the contemner seeks mercy and apology I shall confine to the nature of writing. It can easily be presumed that the writer of the present article, a judicial officer, has considerable knowledge about the law of contempt and for the charges levelled against the Judges of the High Court Division he does not deserve a lenient treatment. "We really do not need such spineless men as Judges." To support this view I, now, may refer to the observation of AR Cornelius, CJ in the following words: "Bearing in mind the nature of an occasion where a highly responsible officer was speaking to others who also were responsible officers, and likely in due time to achieve posts of responsibility not dissimilar to that of the Speaker himself, one would expect that the facts would be stated with the utmost accuracy particularly as criticism was being levelled at an institution of such great importance as the High Court of the country." 

 8. The readers of this Article, specially the unskilled ones in law and ignorant of the judicial functions of the Judges of the Superior Court, will form an impression that Judges of this Court are timid and are incapable to rise to the occasion in performing their duties "at the time of national crisis." Where the writing contains scandalous and unbecoming language to bring the Court into disrespect and disrepute and castigates its dignity, its majesty and challenges its authority specially when the writer has knowledge about the contempt law and working of courts of law he commits contempt of Court. Certainly publication of this article is directed to that end. Ridiculing the performance of a Judge he writes" The High Court Division served show cause notice upon the then Information Minister and later, in pursuance to the doctrine one step forward two steps back it retreated and recalled the notice" and "We really do not need spineless men as Judges. These remarks certainly render the Judges contemptible in the eyes of the general public and undoubtedly casts aspersions on the courage and ability of the Judges and by no stretch of imagination can it be said that it is not written for scandalising the Judges or his authority and does not amount to contempt of court. The article was written malafide in a tone to undermine the judiciary and it tends to breed conflict between the two organs of the state—the legislature and the judiciary in an atomsphere when the whole nation was in a sensitive pulse when the writer writes "And as a matter of fact, the informal Judges are much more powerful than the formal ones." In this regard the following observation of the Supreme Court of Pakistan made in the case of Sir Edward Snelson may be quoted. "In the present case we are concerned with the third kind of contempt. It is committed if there is imputed to the Judges any unfitness, whether on account of incompetence, lack of integrity or otherwise. The essence of this kind of contempt is that the Court is an obstruction to the normal course of justice. The Judges cannot perform their duty properly if they are exposed to libellous attacks. It is necessary as stated by Wilmot J. " to keep a blaze of glory around them and deter people from attempting to render them contemptible in the eyes of the public. " At the same time, it is essential that the confidence of the public in the Courts be maintained." 

 9. To sum up, where a newspaper article attacks the Judges, it is to be seen whether the article has exceeded the limits of fair interference, legitimate comment and criticism. Reading as a whole we find that the article exceeded such limits and tends to scandalise the Judges to lower down their dignity in the estimation of the general public and is calculated to interfere with the administration of justice. The article not only exposes to the public the capacity of the Judges to decide the matter but also tends to prejudice the minds of the Judges to decide the pending Rules issued in the Writ Petitions. In the instant case the writer holds a very poor opinion regarding the capability of the Judges of this Division and it is manifestly clear where he animadverted a particular judgment of High Court Division ridiculing the learned Judge. Where a writing aims to ridicule or tends to ridicule a Judge for his judgments it cannot be termed a fair and corrective criticism and the writer commits contempt of court. Even a fair and liberal reading of the article containing intemperate and offensive language as referred to above in this judgment cannot desist but to hold it as supercilious sarcasm. It seems that any unprejudiced reader will form an impression that the administration of justice is not in safe hands. As the article is full of contumacious writings and considering the attending circumstances the writer is liable to be visited with punishment for committing contempt of Court. 

 11. Now, I take up the case of contemner Nos, 2 and 3. There are cases in which it has been held that where the name of the author is disclosed hardly the Court should hasten to punish contemners. There are cases in which also the Editor functions for editing the article or news item. He writes Editorial Column outside the judicial activities. But it is no excuse or justification to say that they were not aware about the contents of the writing to seek mercy. However, where the writings published are proved to be that of the writer a lenient view may be taken in case of the Editor, the Printer and the Publisher for such news item or the article, as the case may be As in this case contemners 2 and 3 file application for apology and mercy I am satisfied that in view of the statements made therein and attitude and conduct of these contemners in obeying the orders of the Court issued subsequently they deserve a generous consideration. However, it is expected from them that they in future will take sufficient care in matters like the present one. Mr. KZ Alam, the learned Counsel appearing for these contemners, assures us that his clients in future should take sufficient precaution for publishing anything about the conduct and functions of the Judges. In this regard it may be stated that the learned Attorney-General Mr. Aminul Huq, at the time of issuance of the Rule, prayed that no rule should be issued upon these contemners the opposite parties 2-3, as the name of the writer of this article is disclosed. In spite of such prayer Rules were issued to see the conduct and attitude of these contemners towards Judges of the Court. Days together they appeared before this Court personally which is mentioned earlier in this judgment.
